essential to identify a specific element within a set that best meets a certain standard or meets multiple criteria simultaneously. This process, formally recognized as optimization, can be approached by establishing and minimizing a cost function associated with each element in the set. A key characteristic of this method is that the computation for evaluating the cost function at a given point relies solely on local data and does not require access to the entire dataset. This feature becomes especially beneficial when dealing with large datasets, as well as in situations where the set of possible elements is continuous and infinite. A common framework for representing elements in a broad spectrum of problems, including those involving text, images, and scientific data, is through neural network activations. This paper delves into the examination of a particular problem arising from this framework, characterized by a combination of an energy minimization objective and a sparse optimization goal. This is achieved by either analyzing the network in isolation or by employing a pre-trained network and working with an existing weight configuration. Despite being a localized procedure, it is notable that a sparsity-promoting optimization objective can enhance the network's ability to generalize when applied to new data. This research proposes an innovative approach to training a neural network that fully exploits this framework, presenting an efficient method for solving this type of problem using a single pass over the dataset on a parallel computer. This approach effectively addresses the challenge of combining the optimization objective with the sparsity goal in a computationally feasible manner.

multi-phonon physics, is centered on the study of simultaneous creation or annihilation of multiple phonons, which are quantized vibrations of various systems including solids, optical cavities, and nanomechanical devices. This field offers significant applications, for instance, by influencing the structural properties of materials through phonons and employing phonons as carriers of information due to their long lifespan. Presently, however, experiments can only facilitate processes with the creation or annihilation of a small number of phonons, typically one. In contrast, our work surmounts this restriction by demonstrating high-order phonon processes, specifically generating and detecting states with 8 or more phonons simultaneously. By utilizing a bragg reflection scheme, we first create a state containing two photons and two mechanical excitations in an optomechanical system, and then convert the photons into mechanical excitations, resulting in a最终的 state of five to ten identical phonons, which is to our best knowledge, the first demonstration of such high-order states. Our findings will facilitate future studies on multi-phonon physics and its applications.

While this task can be done manually, it is time-consuming and requires skilled radiologists. To make segmentation more efficient, researchers have developed tools that automatically create a training dataset from the original scans by combining patient information and segmentations from multiple areas of the esophagus. These tools typically use a random forest classifier to build the training dataset. In this study, we compare the performance of two methods for generating this training dataset: one based on shape consistency and another based on intensity consistency. We also explore different ways of combining these methods. Our results show that all graph-based approaches significantly improve the accuracy of esophageal tumor segmentation when compared to a basic, non-contour-smoothed method. Furthermore, exploring different ways of combining shape and intensity consistency methods yielded the best accuracy, with an Dice coefficient of 0.741 and a Hausdorff distance of 9.088 mm.

This paper explores the concept of passive bilingualism, where a non-speaker of a particular language can still comprehend that language. This phenomenon can lead to unexpected cases of inaudible code-switching, where a message is sent in one language but understood in another. This phenomenon highlights the limitations of the conventional view that views each speaker's linguistic knowledge as distinct and confined to their own language. To better understand this phenomenon, a new theoretical framework is proposed that views the speaker's communicative intent as multifaceted and not limited to their own linguistic knowledge. a significant challenge for discovering Earth-like planets, as their significant glare is 10 orders of magnitude brighter than our Earth.  Although space-based methods are effective for detecting these habitats, they struggle to identify them around rapidly rotating M dwarfs. In an effort to overcome this shortcoming, we propose a novel approach that involves pre-launching the telescope at the Lagrangian point L4, located roughly 700 thousands kilometers ahead of the parent star.  By implementing this astrodynamical arrangement, we are able to utilize the telescope's starshade to take advantage of the Doppler and gravitational effects to shift the glare outside the telescope's sensitive detection range.  Furthermore, this arrangement enables the detection of the planet's signal through a narrow bandwidth drop outside the telescope.  Using this technique and a 10 meters long baseline, we are able to successfully identify the planet's signature, which is roughly 10 thousands times weaker than the M dwarf's. Although this proposal is specifically designed for M dwarfs, it is also effective for detecting rocky planets orbiting Sun-like stars.  Furthermore, this new approach is adaptable and can be utilized to discover exoplanets around any star.

1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the special linear group GL(n,K) by employing characteristic invariants, specifically utilizing polynomials to identify equivalent conjugacy classes. His work ultimately demonstrated that these invariants are sufficient for distinguishing between different conjugacy classes, although he surprisingy discovered that invariant polynomials alone are not enough, as they do not provide a way to determine if two matrices with identical characteristic invariants are similar. Springer ultimately proved that the kernels associated with characteristic polynomials, along with the number of Jordan blocks sharing the same characteristic polynomial, form the necessary conditions for two matrices to be similar.

Neutrinoless double beta decay represents a neutrino-based nuclear many-body problem, and different theoretical approaches have been developed to explain the complex interactions between numerous protons and neutrons within the nucleus. To address this issue, we systematically compared three prominent nuclear interaction models within the framework of the nuclear shell model. Specifically, for four low-energy experiments, we calculated the decay rates corresponding to three distinct nuclear interaction models and evaluated the sensitivity of the half-life to these many-body model differences. To do this, an estimate of the uncertainty was derived from the variations in calculated rates, and this method of incorporating nuclear model error bars has previously not been applied to this field. As a result, our findings show that the theoretical uncertainty stemming from the choice of nuclear interaction model can contribute significantly to the error bar of any lower bound on the neutrino mass that may be deduced from a future neutrinoless double beta decay experiment.

various image processing tasks, including restoration, enhancement, and synthesis. Nonetheless, these methods typically rely on supervised learning with meticulously annotated datasets, which can be extremely costly and time-consuming to obtain. Although some techniques have been developed for restoration using only imperfect data with minor degradations, they are not applicable to severe image corruption. In this work, we propose a novel framework called the Double Discriminative Generative Adversarial Network (D2GAN) to achieve highly realistic generation from badly corrupted images. The proposed D2GAN consists of two opposing components: a generative adversarial network that creates restoration results using only corrupted images as inputs, and a restoration model trained separately but shares parameters with the decoder. The former enables the D2GAN to generate extremely realistic results, while the latter ensures the basic content structure. The integration of both sides of the decodable information allows the D2GAN to generate results of superior quality from severely corrupted images. Experimental evaluations on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately recover highly distorted content and outperform state-of-the-art methods in terms of restoration quality. The D2GAN's source code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengqiyuan/D2GAN.

problem design holds significant importance, yet it has not been extensively explored. We introduce Matrix Calculus, a framework for developing complex computational problems and corresponding algorithms. Much like non-abelian group theory's role in the creation of puzzles and symmetries, we draw parallels between matrix properties and the underlying structure of problems. By leveraging the linearity feature, we apply the principles of calculus to explore the 'derivative' and 'integral' aspects of matrices, similar to how the study of groups is conducted. This exploration is further supported by an examination of finite fields and the matrix representations of linear operators. We then present the Matrix Calculus Calculator, a computational tool designed to assist in exploring the principles of the framework and identifying areas where the assumptions may not be entirely valid.

tetralogy of Fallot patients is still uncertain due to uncertain symptoms and variable disease progression. We studied the pulmonary valve status in 129 tetralogy of Fallot patients who didn't require surgery due to pulmonary valve failure. We analyzed echocardiographic data, including the peak regurgitant velocity, right ventricular peak pressure, and pulmonary valve regurgitant orifice area, from these patients at their initial examination and tracked it for an average of 8.4 years. We identified distinct disease progression patterns based on peak regurgitant velocity and categorized them into slow, moderate, and rapid groups. Patients with slow progression had average clinical survival rates similar to those without fallot, indicating that pulmonary valve replacement surgery could be timed later. Patients with moderate or rapid progression had average fallot-like survival rates, requiring pulmonary valve replacement surgery at or before average clinical survival rate divergence. Our findings offer pulmonary valve fallot-specific patients longer-term insights, supporting tailored management and potentially delayed surgery, improving quality of life and survival outcomes.

The system combines point-to-point and broadcast connections to create a flexible network that can support faster data transfer and more sustainable energy consumption. By point-to-point harvesting, a part of transmitted energy can be recovered from both sender and receiver, while broadcast harvesting uses the broadcast channel to transmit information to multiple users and recovered energy for further use. A new optimization problem is developed to maximize system efficiency by determining the optimal information and energy transmission rates, subject to certain constraints. Pyramid Networks (FPN), have experienced notable advancements in the community. FPN addresses the challenge of scale variability by combining bottom-up and top-down loop pathways to produce rich feature maps for objects at different sizes. Currently, most applications run these networks on single-GPU systems; however, such systems have limited computing capabilities compared to their multi-GPU counterparts. In this study, we introduce an innovative approach called HIFP-N (Heterogeneous Integrated Feature Pyramid Network) that adaptably combines the features from each level of the FPN using both bottom-up and top-down paths when using multiple GPUs in a heterogeneous environment. By integrating feature pyramids with heterogeneous systems, we achieve not only improved computational efficiency but also better detection results. For instance, HIFP-N showcases an 11.2% increase in detection accuracy and an 11.2% reduction in detection time when evaluated on the MS COCO dataset in comparison to the original FPN.

In this paper, we introduce a unified framework for estimating and estimating the density of conditional distributions at their boundaries, enabling precise estimation of extreme probabilities within a specified level of rarity, and we also present a novel summary metric to rank the density at the boundaries, making it applicable to various conditional models, and we provide a detailed demonstration of our methodology with examples from different models, and we propose the use of a Monte Carlo approach to estimate the bias present in our framework, ultimately, our method can be applied to a wide range of conditional models, including but not limited to, Bayesian networks, Markov chains, Gaussian Markov random fields, exponential random graphs, and exponential random lates.

iguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to build upon and improve previous work, particularly Huang et al.'s Gloss-Based WSD approach, we introduce a series of innovations to address limitations in their methodology. First, we address the issue of unavailable sense-tagged sentences by identifying relevant disambiguated sentences from WordNet 3.1. Secondly, we expand the set of possible disambiguous words by incorporating terms from related words, which can provide additional clues for disambiguating word meanings. Finally, we develop a more sophisticated representation of surrounding context sentences, namely a bag-of-bags-of-words structure, which captures hierarchical relationships between words. Our enhancements lead to considerable performance gains on the SemCor corpus, yielding an overall accuracy of 71.1%, a 5.4% improvement over the original approach.

common task that underlies understanding more complex narratives. Previous studies typically focus on events with a linear order and require events to be described and arranged in a correct sequential description. In contrast, events in everyday life rarely fit into such a straightforward pattern. Our new task, Chaotic Events Ordering, requires participants to describe and provide a logically coherent sequence of events, which may involve multiple points in time and are presented in an unordered format. Three experiments were used to investigate how the brain represents and processes events in a linear and chaotic context. Results indicate that both contexts activate areas associated with language production and sequence processing, but the chaotic context activates additional areas related to spatial reasoning and working memory. fMRI imaging further confirmed these findings by showing increased activity in parietal lobe areas during the chaotic events condition. Our research has significant implications for our understanding of the cognitive processes involved in comprehending and producing narrative accounts of complex, unordered events.

Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures like network connectivity, without examining how individual nodes contribute to vulnerability. In this research, we developed a node-specific vulnerability measure that reflects the node's susceptibility to failure, using concepts from percolation theory and network component structure. Through both analytical and simulation methods, we found that this node-based approach provides a more detailed understanding of network vulnerability, particularly in relation to node centrality and the thresholds required for network connectivity. Additionally, we demonstrated the practical value of this measure in creating strategies to mitigate the spread of infectious diseases and malicious information, outperforming traditional centrality-based methods.

As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions that create a complex and abruptly changing small-scale fading pattern. Moreover, due to excessive background noise at room temperature, high-gain antennas are prone to thermal noise. To address these challenges, we develop a new noise-aware channel model that incorporates a precise model of the frequency-dependent effective noise temperature. Based on these considerations, we propose a novel total SNR model that accounts for thermal noise, and conduct a comprehensive performance analysis of the practical applications of MIMO through our custom-designed model. Through the evaluation of data rates and regularizations in our simulations, we demonstrate the necessity of incorporating both the abrupt changes in MIMO channel realizations and the limitations imposed by thermal noise.

Sketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch is sensitive to inputs that already have few large components, limiting its practical usage. In contrast, the new LimitedMaxSketch sketch is designed to robustly extract the top components of a vector's squared magnitude by mapping only the portions exceeding a certain dynamic threshold, which adapts to each input measurement. The new threshold-based sketch can be viewed as a specialized form of a broader (and previously unknown) measurement technique that identifies the top components of a vector exceeding a certain threshold in any highly dimensional space. The new limited maximum sketch employs minimal randomness per column within the measurement matrix, a distinctive feature setting it apart from previous linear measurement methods. Notably, the new limited maximum sketch achieves efficiency by reusing existing CountSketch sketches with redundant columns, a capability that cannot be easily accomplished by non-specialized measurement methods.

strategic deployment of aggregators, yet designing optimal aggregation policies poses significant challenges. These policies need to respect diverse and sometimes conflicting constraints related to individual control units, customer comfort, market dynamics, and grid stability. Given the intricate nature of real-world energy systems, this problem rapidly escalates in complexity. To tackle this issue, we frame it within a hierarchical model, where aggregators take on the role of intermediaries between control units and the grid operator. Each aggregator aims to meet its own performance objectives while guaranteeing that its control units' requirements are met. We explore this model through a case study of temperature setpoints for heating systems. Initially, each control unit's constraints are localized within its respective aggregator. Subsequently, these localized constraints are used to inform an optimization problem managed by the grid operator. Despite potential benefits, this approach introduces issues of operator autonomy restriction and performance degradation. To mitigate these concerns, we introduce a suite of cost functions designed to encapsulate the complexity of control units' requirements, enabling more manageable management of energy consumption units.

attributed to rising participation in day trading.  Day trading is a short-term trading strategy where securities are bought and/or sold on the same day within which the trade is made.  A key feature of this approach is its reliance on intraday data, characterized by unusually volatile and uneven patterns.  Due to its complex nature, accurately predicting the market's behavior within a single day is challenging, particularly when using regression-based techniques that often struggle with the problem's non-linear nature.  In an effort to address the issue, numerous studies have applied a wide range of machine learning models to develop effective end-day direction classifiers.  However, no research to date has systematically compared the performance of multiple machine learning algorithms in this context.  To bridge this gap, our study compares the performance of ten machine learning models designed to determine the market's end-of-day trend, with all models being fed the same set of intraday features.  Our comparative analysis reveals that ensemble tree-based methods, in particular, outperform other alternatives, offering a valuable insight for day traders in navigating the efficiency of various model architectures.  Moreover, our analysis highlights several significant end-of-day trading opportunities, characterized by substantial returns, low risks, and high levels of accuracy.

As a result, LIGO and Virgo should be able to detect these particles by comparing the observed waveform with classical predictions and placing constraints on the abundance of these particles in the vicinity of the gravitational wave sources based on the waveform analysis, particularly in cases where the particles are concentrated around the location of the gravitational wave event.

a primary criterion, which measures the extent of change in the potential energy landscape, characterized by its sharpness. A statistical thermodynamic method has been developed to quantify this criterion, enabling an analysis of typical energy barriers, their distribution, and barriers that pose obstacles to forward progression. This approach is applicable to various process types, both abrupt and smooth, and has been utilized to examine the thermodynamic underpinnings of barrier heights in model scenarios, including the over-the-barrier requirement and tunneling reactions. A reaction threshold, where tunneling ceases to be advantageous, can also be identified through this analysis. A sudden decrease in the distribution of barriers that hinder forward progression is observed in the thermodynamic regime, in contrast to the extended distribution of barriers found in the kinetic regime. A key component of these achievements is gradient-based optimization, an iterative method used to minimize a cost function. This method involves making incremental adjustments to the network's parameters, but calculating the impact of each adjustment across all network connections is both time-consuming and computationally expensive. This challenge can exacerbate issues with scalability, leading to difficulties in training large artificial neural networks. This research presents a novel, efficient approach to computing the effect of parameter adjustments on a function, utilizing a specialized, localized algebraic structure. By leveraging this method, the proposed alternative optimization system, known as NOIS, utilizes a non-gradient-based system to efficiently retrain large, complex artificial neural networks by replacing parameter adjustments with localized changes during retraining. Initial experimental results indicate that NOIS can effectively overcome scalability challenges, successfully retraining even the largest, state-of-the-art artificial neural networks.

long been a gold standard for geophysical exploration, yet its applications are becoming limited due to the need for high-quality data and expensive field operations. In light of these challenges, natural imaging techniques using seismic waves have emerged as an energy-efficient and field-independent alternative. Although this method provides accurate estimates of structural features and wave speeds, it yields ambiguous results and is ineffective in locating absolute minima. To overcome these shortcomings, researchers are incorporating regularizing terms, like smoothness constraints, but this can lead to artificially uniform solutions. To address this issue, recent studies have utilized nonconvex regularization methods, such as total variation (TV) and wavefront reversal imaging (WRI). However, these methods have limitations in predicting earth models with varying densities and seismic sources. To overcome these challenges, we developed a novel approach, wavefront reversal total variation imaging (WRTV), which integrates the wavefront reversal method and TV regularization to produce a more detailed and geologically plausible estimate of underground structures. To handle density variations and inelastic media effects, we modified our approach to account for these factors in a specific type of wave equation. Additionally, to address scenarios with unknown sources, we developed an adaptive version of our method that uses multiple sources to obtain a more accurate underground model estimate.

Current neural embedding methods, though effective, fail to capture the intricate relationships between words and do not provide a solid foundation for human-comprehensible analysis. In contrast, composite embedding approaches, such as attention mechanisms, produce ensembles of sentence-level representations, but significantly increase the computational cost, resulting in less practical applications. In this research, we introduce a novel EA$^2$ model, which integrates the advantages of composite embedding and produces a lexicalized, human-interpretable, comparative, and dynamic language representation, all at a computational cost comparable to that of baseline models. The EA$^2$ model exhibits unparalleled efficiency, delivering state-of-the-art performance in embedding evaluation benchmarks, and outshines established comparative models in both evaluated metrics and computational cost. Furthermore, the EA$^2$ model shows state-of-the-art efficacy in pragmatic dialogue tasks, highlighting the suitability of its produced semantics for effective conversational interactions. The source code for the EA$^2$ model is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengqian1995/EQEA-model.

Unsupervised learning for 3D point clouds remains an open challenge, largely because point clouds lack semantic information and have complex, repetitive backgrounds. To tackle this, we introduce a novel unsupervised3D traffic and scene representation learning framework that directly processes3D LiDAR data, utilizing two primary components. The first component applies a simple frequency filtering technique to separate the high and low frequency information, effectively isolating foreground and background information. The second component employs a contrastive learning technique to learn more discriminative representations. We experiment with various modifications of the low frequency filtering technique and evaluate our framework on two public LiDAR datasets, the MOSS and SUID datasets, in a fully unsupervised learning setting. Our results demonstrate that our framework achieves remarkable performance, setting a new state-of-the-art in 3D LiDAR-driven traffic and scene representation learning.

Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) is the most effective algorithm for predicting and managing video requests, but it suffers from high computational costs, especially when dealing with the increasing data rates in network operator systems.

This research project seeks to fill the gap by examining whether individuals are influenced in their drug abuse habits by the habits of people in their social circle. To protect users' data, prior approaches take advantage of diverse platforms like cloud computing, trusted third parties, and secure multi-party computation. In contrast to these methods that rely on external systems, this research proposes utilizing homomorphic encryption to achieve privacy protection within personal devices. studying a striking visual phenomenon called the rainbow effect, first documented on the surface of rotating planets like Jupiter and Saturn. The effect arises from the dispersion of sunlight into its component colors by clouds composed of spherical particles, and has been observed on the surfaces of the Gas Giants as well as in laboratory settings and on the surfaces of asteroids. Notably, the coloration on the Gas Giants appears six to seven orders of magnitude brighter than on the asteroids, underscoring the significance of research on rainbow formation. Despite numerous related phenomena being documented, there has not, until now, been a single framework that unifies an understanding of all these phenomena. By applying the ray-optics approach, our study derives the Mie theory from first principles and identifies the critical component of rainbows, known as the rainbow cusp in the scattering pattern, which marks a discontinuity in the ray-optics approximation. The rainbow cusp results from the accumulation of rays tangent to an envelope defined by the ray impact angles. In addition, we explore various phenomena created by other ray accumulations tangent to different types of envelopes, including ray caustics. The study also covers the ray impingent caustic, which has implications for the cusp shadows and the brightness of rainbows. Furthermore, the study discusses the formation of rainbows on non-spherical particles, irregular surfaces, and rotating gas giants, and analyzes the conditions necessary for the appearance of the rainbow cusp on the object's surface. Although there are tools available to resolve acronyms, they rely heavily on pre-defined knowledge, limiting their broader application. By focusing on these connections, we can effectively resolve not only standard acronyms, but also novel ones encountered for the first time. This method also enables us to identify reverse acronyms formed from shortened technical terms. To accomplish this, we propose a unified framework that incorporates a low-shot and a zero-shot setting. The low-shot setting involves training the model on actual acronyms, whereas the zero-shot setting requires it to locate any short expression corefering with a longer one, regardless of its nature. affects both macroscopic and microscopic systems, and it plays a significant role in numerous natural and technological applications. Despite its widespread impact, accurately predicting the influence of the quantum vacuum within these diverse settings remains a significant challenge. Quantum Electrodynamics in the Fundamental State (QED-in-the-vacuum) is used to model the quantum vacuum, and while it has been extensively applied to both condensed matter and low-energy quantum chromodynamics (LYQCDD), there are very few QED-in-the-vacuum LYQCDD applications. This study focuses on LYQCDD, quantizing the electromagnetic field and hadron sources separately, and emphasizes the importance of hadron sources in explaining the proton's spin. To do this, we employ the proton's spin sum as an example and apply the Gasser-Leutwyler (GL) expansion to the hadron source's correlation function's second order, and as a result, we are able to calculate the axial charge $a_0$ in the proton's spin sum.

Studying such systems is greatly facilitated by identifying and analyzing "simple states" that remain stable under standard dynamics and can be understood through conventional means. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures and drug-resistant epilepsy by employing laser energy to thermally destroy brain tissue seizures originate from. The difficulty lies in unpredictable seizure-triggering locations in epilepsy patients, making precise preoperative planning challenging. Our research tackles this challenge by developing a method to identify potential epileptic focus areas based on individual patient characteristics. We apply a diffusion process with stochastic influences to model the brain tissue, generating a probability map of seizure-triggering areas. A innovative, cost-effective, real-time, boundary-controlling method is then employed to treat this probability map using a level-set approach. The results show that our approach can accurately handle large, irregular boundaries at a significantly lower computational cost compared to standard techniques. Moreover, our approach allows for the preservation of crucial anatomical features while reshaping the epileptic focus, leading to improved patient outcomes. The proposed technique can also guide LITT treatment by identifying untreated focus areas.

This phenomenon, where a model performs well despite a net benefit that exceeds what's expected, is prevalent in NLP tasks and is expected to persist with more large-scale neural models. free lunch effect can be understood through a variation of Occam's razor, favoring simpler hypotheses that make fewer assumptions, which is maximum likelihood essentially assuming. The result involves multiple power-law components, with similar but distinct properties for shock waves impacting a universe with different matter compositions. When a shock wave hits a universe dominated by slow expansion, it behaves according to a square cube root power law, while in a matter-dominated universe, it follows a four-thirds power law. The standard practice of discarding subjects with any missing values biases time-sensitivity parameter estimates, which can be overly or inappropriately conservative. Our proposed solution is a robust R function that corrects this issue by accounting for the Monotone Missing data pattern, prevalent in public health studies. This solution employs a Weighted Estimating Equation (WEE) approach, utilizing an inverse probability weighting method to achieve unbiased and efficient estimates under specific conditions. However, the effectiveness of this strategy is constrained by the monotonically increasing nature of the missing data pattern. Furthermore, we highlight that in typical public health studies, this pattern does not reflect the actual missing data structure, thus rendering our initial solution potentially biased and inefficient. A more flexible alternative solution is presented, capable of addressing more realistic missing data patterns, although it comes with increased computational complexity.

In this study, we introduce an alternative and streamlined design for robustly supervised reward signals that aligns with CNN architecture and leverages human-comprehensible image understanding. Specifically, we introduce a forward model that predicts object locations from generic images and finds a balance between performance and computational efficiency. By leveraging pre-trained CNN models like Places200, we extract a compact and comprehensible representation of visual similarity, which has been shown to excel in zero-shot classification. Integrating these two components yields a highly performant and lightweight system that surpasses state-of-the-line approaches in terms of planning accuracy and efficiency, all while utilizing depth-free, natural-image-based reward signals in a single forward pass. As a result, our method exhibits exceptional performance, highest accuracy and efficiency, and the ability to generalize to new environments with minimal tuning, all while using a simple and compact model that outperforms state-of-the-line methods in terms of computational efficiency, whether it be 7x or 10x faster.

Basic graph coloring involves assigning colors to vertices, ensuring adjacent vertices have different colors. A more complex variant is list coloring where each vertex has a predefined color option list and must be colored with one of those colors. A key paper exploring list coloring effects was published by Kim, Oum, and Seroussi at the SODA conference, which investigated colored edges and showed that graph coloring relates to certain connectivity measures, similar to the property that (k+1)- colorable graphs are easily connected but k-colorable graphs are hard to connect. Building on this, the authors showed that a broader version of this relationship exists where connectivity is related to the 'choosability' of graphs, which extends list coloring to vertices with larger color options lists. Also, they proved a quantitative version of the Thompson-Tuza conjecture, providing nearly optimal bounds for disconnected k-list-colorable graphs with limited average list sizes, which had previously been asked about. Also, they confirmed a long-standing hypothesis related to planar graphs that are 5- list-colorable when faces are considered in the connectivity measure, but showed some hypotheses requiring 3-list-colorability are incorrect. Also, they found that outerplanar graphs are always connected 2-k-colorable but some graphs requiring more than 2-k total colorability exist.

The Async Federated Learning approach mitigates this issue by allowing devices to contribute at different times, but this introduces the problem of inconsistent updates which can substantially decrease the model's accuracy. Although existing solutions try to address this issue without increasing the communication overhead, they often converge slowly. In contrast, we propose two penalty-based methods that incorporate the consistency issue as an optimization problem. The first method uses a global penalty coefficient that acts as a form of momentum to improve convergence speed, but requires increased communication to exchange coefficient updates. The second method employs a local penalty coefficient to avoid additional communication, but may lead to update misalignment and affect convergence speed. Furthermore, we establish theoretical bounds on convergence for DFED learning and demonstrate through simulations that our methods are more efficient and achieve higher accuracy in comparison to other penalty-based methods and traditional optimization algorithms.

details of their discovered security flaws and potential exploitation methods, 
commercial companies often keep the full details of the vulnerabilities they 
found confidential. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for 
analyzing the security flaw disclosure practices of cybersecurity firms, using the 
examples of HackerOne and Bugcrowd. The proposed framework centers around nine 
key evaluation criteria, focusing on the depth of analysis, clear description 
of the security flaw, and the ability to reproduce the issue. HoneEval, a 
automated framework for assessing these disclosure practices by analyzing the 
reviews submitted during vulnerability submission campaigns, uses advanced 
natural language processing techniques to extract semantic features and perform 
multi-label classification. The use of these techniques enables the assessment 
of the overall quality of security flaw descriptions, along with the ability 
to reproduce the issue and identify affected users. This paper presents experiments 
conducted across 17 real-world campaigns that demonstrate the effectiveness 
of HoneEval in accurately assessing security flaw disclosures.

Traditional PVDFs are designed for credible users and are vulnerable to malicious server attacks. In contrast, our extended model TPVDFs operate under a malicious server assumption, allowing for secure computations by publicly auditability features. Specifically, TPVDFs possess the properties of correctly generating the f(k,1)^(f(k,2)...(f(k,n))) value from input k and public auditability, which guarantees the necessary properties of PVDFs, including the containment property. Our lower bound analysis reveals that any TPDF under the malicious security assumption is at least as computationally complex as NP-complete problems, implying that RSA and elliptic curve-based NIPVDFs are not computationally feasible as TPVDFs. Nevertheless, we propose a new MPVDV based on the Discrete Logarithm problem that is both secure against malicious servers and publicly auditable.

However, the complexity of these processes, which are influenced by charge effects and reactions on non-neutral surfaces, makes it challenging to study. In this research, we identify key factors affecting reactions between volatile and water-soluble substances by developing a quantitative model and conducting both charged droplet evaporation tests using laser-induced breakdown and gas-phase tests. Our results from comparing these experiments reveal the impact of charge on the conversion of one substance into another, with the charged droplet tests producing significantly higher yields. Both tests at 300K and 420K show a marked difference in the conversion results, with the latter showing a much higher yield in the converted product. The increased charge also leads to a higher concentration of a related substance within the droplets. The laser tests allow for the measurement of this related substance's cross-section as it enters the droplets, with the charged droplet tests producing approximately ten times higher results. The increased charge additionally reduces the minimum size at which two molecules can approach and react, with this effect being particularly evident in the420K tests.

GPU technology and advanced solvers like FAS multigrid, have significantly accelerated the simulation of compressible turbulence on coarse scales. However, capturing high-resolution turbulent flows remains challenging due to limited computational resources. Existing methods such as adaptive mesh refinement and field operator-based approaches have achieved some success, but at considerable computational costs, making direct pixel-based simulation the gold standard. Despite our FAS multigrid algorithm's efficiency, a key difference between it and traditional implementations remains: FAS employs a time-parallel approach using a dual-space domain decomposition method, while standard algorithms use sequential time-stepping. To explore how this distinction affects performance, we compare time-parallel and sequential FAS multigrid algorithms, finding that while the time-parallel version offers some speedup, neither matches pixel-based simulation's performance. To analyze the cause, we investigate the error properties of convection and diffusion operators, the impact of high-frequency fluctuations, and conduct a novel energy-based analysis of the FAS multigrid algorithm, ultimately revealing that mass transport across the refinement interface is crucial for solution convergence.

Although various image processing and machine learning techniques have been developed for automatic medical image analysis, these methods can't fully replace human expertise. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. Although recent advancements in neural network technology have significantly boosted the accuracy of learning nonlinear Hawkes process models, they often result in complex multi-type event models with numerous connections that are challenging to interpret. We introduce a simplified class of nonlinear models called sparse linear-hawkes processes that are based on the linear Hawkes process and feature sparse connections between events, enabling them to reduce model complexity and improve interpretability. We also develop an efficient algorithm to estimate a sparse linear-hawkes process model by combining sparse regularization with the maximum likelihood estimation method. To evaluate the performance of our proposed approach, we conduct a simulation study to assess the sparsity of learned connections between events and apply the estimated models to the analysis of events, including online forum posts and Facebook comments.

However discrepancies arise in angular momentum conservation due to an inherently non-symmetric tensor in the particle pressure calculation. This nonphysical behavior induces spurious rotations in isolated systems. However, when these models are evaluated for security, they were typically tested for their vulnerability to adversarial examples, which fool them into misclassifying modified images, and backdoors, which cause them to classify specific, undetectable images incorrectly, and supply chains, which involve the compromise of software during distribution. What this assessment overlooked was the phenomenon of natural backdoors, which occur without any malicious intent. These can be activated by simply retraining popular image classification models on commonly available, unfiltered internet data, and they can be triggered by certain common types of images, such as those containing watermarks.

Using data collected from 11 U.S. cities, researchers investigated how noise levels affect public park usage, combining acoustic simulations with GPS trajectory data and social demographic information. Their analysis, accounting for various control variables, indicates that park visitors are more likely to stay away from quieter areas, seemingly drawn to noisier parts of the parks. Surprisingly, they are also more willing to tolerate higher background noise when present in smaller groups. Notably, park users are less inclined to initiate conversations in quieter, tree-filled areas of the parks. The research also offers policy recommendations for mitigating the impact of noise on park usage.

Here, fluid permeability varies randomly, impacting how fluid flows through the rock. We've adopted a common strategy of analyzing fluid flow over large areas first, considering time as the primary factor. Our study instead takes a more detailed approach, focusing on small spaces where we can explore the interaction between fluid properties and the rock surface. Our results provide a new perspective on the study of fluid flow in rock systems and contribute to a better understanding of processes like fluid transport and chemical reactions in complex environments.

in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), where the inflow of gas is influenced by both local and global dynamics. Their analysis focused on four non-overlapping fields in the inner CMZ, allowing them to compare process-interactions against each other. Comparing the line ratios between four fields enabled the assessment of dust heating differences caused by varying local conditions, as well as gas flow patterns dictated by both local and global forces. Their results indicated that the dust heating in these gases was not uniform, suggesting its dependence on both local and global dynamics. Additionally, they discovered signs of gas inflow in three of the four fields studied, as well as a correlation between N2H+ line ratios and the gas density, suggesting that gas flow patterns within the CMZ are influenced by both local and global dynamics. Their analysis also pointed to the need for further research on N2H+ line ratios in the outer CMZ to better understand gas flow's global dynamics.

Recently, certain natural compounds have been shown to induce pyroptosis in cells, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Notably, ginsenoside Rh2 (G Rh2) has demonstrated potent anti-tumor and anti-infectious properties. However, no studies have examined the effect of G Rh2 on pyroptotic cell death caused by SARS-CoV-2. Using techniques such as immunofluorescence, western blotting, and real-time PCR, our research discovered that G Rh2 indeed induces pyroptotic cell death in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells by activating the NLRP3 inflammasome, confirmed by the release of IL-1β, IL-18, and gdh2 proteins as well as the accumulation of acridine orange. Moreover, this process is mediated through G Rh2's inhibition of ACYD5 expression, which in turn reduces ACYD5's suppression of NLRP3. These mechanisms were validated using molecular simulations. These discoveries provide valuable insights into how G Rh2 induces pyroptotic cell death in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells, which is essential for evaluating G Rh2's potential clinical applications.

Recent research has shown that the standard GCN-based node classification methods can be improved by incorporating additional labels from unlabelled nodes. However, these approaches typically rely on heavily labelled 'hub' nodes, leaving the majority of 'non-hub' nodes without sufficient labels. Non-hub nodes, although abundant, are characterized by overlapping class features, which can be effectively utilized in a mutual learning framework to enhance each other's understanding. Nevertheless, hub nodes and non-hub nodes differ significantly in their label density and feature overlap, which can negatively impact the mutual learning process. To overcome this challenge, a novel mutual learning-based GCN (nMLGCN) is proposed, which employs a selective mutual learning mechanism to dynamically exchange knowledge between non-hub nodes and utilize a soft label generation mechanism to create pseudo labels for unlabelled nodes. The experimental results on the Cora, CiteSeer, and PubMed datasets demonstrate that nMLGCN consistently achieves superior performance compared to existing methods. The source code for nMLGCN is available on GitHub.
